A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Force Prompting work and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Existing material can be matched across pagination changes and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original human evaluations in Tables 1–2, mass-response measurements in Figure 6, and qualitative experiments and ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds multiple-force experiments, joint local/global training results, and a reduced-training-data ablation.

M1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds a multiple-force inference adaptation using one Gaussian blob per applied force. Appendix C.3 adds a unified local/wind model trained with equally mixed batches. These are limited procedural extensions; the original force encodings and six-layer ControlNet architecture remain.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds simultaneous local-force control on six two-object scenes and simultaneous mass-response tests with baskets and books. This extends task requirements beyond the earlier single-force evaluations. The original training domains and 63-image local and 41-image global benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain the same comparators: text-only zero-shot, text-only fine-tuned, Motion Prompting, and PhysDreamer. The appendix's qualitative simulator comparison list is also unchanged. Newly cited Wonderplay and PhysCtrl are not added evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce four force-direction pairings per two-object scene, paired-object mass tests over eight force magnitudes, 50/50 local/wind training batches, and a half-size wind dataset with unchanged training steps and scheduler. These supplement the retained principal evaluations. Appendix A.4 documents the existing PhysDreamer comparison rather than establishing a changed protocol.

E4.justification: Appendices C.3–C.4 add targeted qualitative analyses of joint versus separate force training and sensitivity to halving the wind training dataset. Appendix B also probes compositional force and mass generalization. The earlier diversity, distractor, keyword, failure, and emergent-behavior analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies one generated video per prompt using the same seed throughout the multiple-force experiment. Existing reporting of ten differently seeded videos per force value in the quantitative mass study and four seeds in the qualitative mass study remains unchanged. No new uncertainty estimates are supplied.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 6 retain their results. Added findings include multiple-force adherence, mass-dependent motion within paired-object scenes, more dynamic backgrounds but weaker local control after joint training, and additional half-data failures. Appendix B.1 reports '5/6 of the videos' with perfect adherence, but its six-scene, four-prompts-per-scene design leaves that denominator unclear.

T1.justification: The formal force representations in Section 3.2 and Gaussian-blob displacement formula in Appendix A.3 are unchanged. The added experiments introduce no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: learning force control from limited synthetic data, generalizing without a simulator at inference, and exhibiting some mass understanding. The supplementary findings do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C.4 newly interprets reduced-data hallucinations as possible memorization of waving-flag patterns and partial confetti responses as weaker generalization. Joint training adds a qualification about reduced local-control robustness. Existing limitations concerning the base video prior and unsuitability for precise physical simulation remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.4 explains the existing PhysDreamer comparison's annotation-free screenshots, matched force vectors, Qualtrics presentation, and left/right randomization. Appendix A.1 changes the stated available transformer-block count from eight to 42 while retaining six copied blocks. Added experiments also document control construction and batch composition; resource-access claims remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the references add Wonderplay and PhysCtrl, distinguishing their simulator-at-inference and learned 3D trajectory approaches from Force Prompting. This is a limited expansion of concurrent-work positioning; the existing related-work discussion is otherwise retained.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged. v2 adds appendix subsections and a dedicated multiple-force appendix, reletters subsequent appendices, and inserts brief main-text references to the additions. Smaller edits expand HDRI and add conference and acknowledgment text.

P2.justification: Figure 3 gains a multiple-forces row, adjusted spacing, and a caption explanation of the blue motion lines. Other figures and table structures are retained. Pagination redistributes text and floats, including placing the two survey screenshots on separate pages.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly strengthens the paper through multiple-force generalization evidence, informative joint-training and dataset-size analyses, and clearer documentation of the PhysDreamer comparison. The principal benchmark results remain unchanged. The additions are mostly qualitative, and the single-seed multiple-force test has an unclear '5/6 videos' denominator, limiting the strength of the added evidence.
